expectedText:
GENERAL PARTNER FIDUCIARY DUTIES IN A CALIFORNIA LIMITED PARTNERSHIP — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Ventures, LP

IDENTIFICATION
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee, general partner of Acme Ventures, LP, a California limited partnership, and Casey Alex, a limited partner of that limited partnership. It addresses the fiduciary duties that California's Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 assigns to a general partner, and the extent to which the limited partnership's own partnership agreement may narrow those duties.

THE TWO STATUTORY FIDUCIARY DUTIES
California's limited partnership statute states that a general partner's fiduciary duties to the limited partnership and to the other partners consist of exactly two duties — a duty of loyalty and a duty of care — and that each of those duties is defined and limited by a separate subdivision of the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The fiduciary duties that a general partner owes to the limited partnership and the other partners are the duties of loyalty and care under subdivisions (b) and (c)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the two fiduciary duties a general partner owes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15904.08.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(a), the introductory sentence identifying the two duties. It does not state the content of either duty, which the companion clauses of this document address separately by quoting subdivisions (b) and (c). It does not address whether a general partner that is itself an entity (for example, a corporation or LLC serving as general partner) owes these duties through its own directors, managers, or officers, a question the statute does not answer in this subdivision. No case law was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search for California opinions citing this section by name returned no results, so this document does not represent that any court has construed subdivision (a).

DUTY OF LOYALTY: ACCOUNTING FOR PROPERTY, PROFIT, AND LIMITED PARTNERSHIP OPPORTUNITIES
The first component of a general partner's statutory duty of loyalty is an accounting duty: the general partner must account to the limited partnership, and hold as trustee for it, any property, profit, or benefit the general partner derives in the conduct or winding up of the limited partnership's activities, or derives from using limited partnership property — and the statute specifically includes within this duty the appropriation of a limited partnership opportunity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "to account to the limited partnership and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the general partner in the conduct and winding up of the limited partnership’s activities or derived from a use by the general partner of limited partnership property, including the appropriation of a limited partnership opportunity"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, accounting for property, profit, or benefit including appropriation of a limited partnership opportunity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15904.08.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(b)(1). It does not define what makes an opportunity a "limited partnership opportunity" for purposes of the appropriation rule, a line-drawing question the statute leaves to case-by-case application. It does not address the partnership agreement's power to narrow this duty by identifying categories of activity that do not violate it or by authorizing specific transactions in advance, which a separate clause of this document addresses (id: lpgpduty_agreement_cannot_eliminate_loyalty, citing Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(5)). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

DUTY OF LOYALTY: REFRAINING FROM ADVERSE-INTEREST DEALING
The second component of the statutory duty of loyalty requires a general partner to refrain from dealing with the limited partnership, in the conduct or winding up of its activities, as or on behalf of a party whose interest is adverse to the limited partnership's own interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "to refrain from dealing with the limited partnership in the conduct or winding up of the limited partnership’s activities as or on behalf of a party having an interest adverse to the limited partnership"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, refraining from adverse-interest dealing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15904.08.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(b)(2). It does not define what makes an interest "adverse," nor does it address whether or how the partnership agreement's ratification mechanism (a separate clause of this document, id: lpgpduty_agreement_cannot_eliminate_loyalty, citing § 15901.10(b)(5)(B)) can authorize a specific adverse-interest transaction after full disclosure. It does not address remedies for a violation of this component. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

DUTY OF LOYALTY: REFRAINING FROM COMPETING WITH THE LIMITED PARTNERSHIP
The third component of the statutory duty of loyalty requires a general partner to refrain from competing with the limited partnership in the conduct or winding up of its activities.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "to refrain from competing with the limited partnership in the conduct or winding up of the limited partnership’s activities"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, refraining from competing with the limited partnership (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15904.08.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(b)(3). It does not define what constitutes "competing" with the limited partnership, does not address whether the partnership agreement can carve out specific competitive activities in advance (a separate clause of this document, id: lpgpduty_agreement_cannot_eliminate_loyalty, addresses that general mechanism), and does not address any duty that might continue, or end, after the general partner dissociates. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

DUTY OF CARE: A GROSS-NEGLIGENCE STANDARD
The statutory duty of care owed by a general partner to the limited partnership and the other partners, in the conduct and winding up of the limited partnership's activities, is limited to refraining from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law. Ordinary negligence, standing alone, is not stated as a basis for a duty-of-care violation under this subdivision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A general partner’s duty of care to the limited partnership and the other partners in the conduct and winding up of the limited partnership’s activities is limited to refraining from engaging in grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the duty-of-care standard for a general partner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15904.08.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(c). It does not define "grossly negligent," "reckless," or "knowing violation of law" beyond the statute's own words, and it does not address the partnership agreement's power to reduce this standard further, which is limited by a separate provision (a companion clause of this document, id: lpgpduty_agreement_care_and_good_faith_limits, citing Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(6), which permits reducing but not "unreasonably" reducing this duty). No case law construing this specific subdivision was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search for California opinions applying this gross-negligence standard to a limited partnership general partner returned no on-point results within the scope of this research.

THE OBLIGATION OF GOOD FAITH AND FAIR DEALING, AND THE SELF-INTEREST CARVE-OUT
Beyond the two named fiduciary duties, the statute separately requires a general partner to discharge its duties to the partnership and other partners, and to exercise any of its rights, consistently with an obligation of good faith and fair dealing. The statute then adds a limiting principle: a general partner does not violate a duty or obligation merely because its conduct furthers the general partner's own interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A general partner shall discharge the duties to the partnership and the other partners under this chapter or under the partnership agreement and exercise any rights consistently with the obligation of good faith and fair dealing."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the good faith and fair dealing obligation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15904.08.)
  "A general partner does not violate a duty or obligation under this chapter or under the partnership agreement merely because the general partner’s conduct furthers the general partner’s own interest."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, self-interested conduct alone is not a violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15904.08.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(d) and (e). It does not define "good faith and fair dealing" beyond the statute's own words, and it does not resolve how the self-interest carve-out in subdivision (e) interacts with the specific duty-of-loyalty prohibitions in subdivision (b) — for example, whether conduct that both furthers the general partner's own interest and independently breaches subdivision (b)(2)'s adverse-interest rule is excused by subdivision (e) or still prohibited by subdivision (b). The statute's text does not itself resolve that interaction, and no case law was independently researched for this clause.

WHAT THE PARTNERSHIP AGREEMENT MAY NOT DO: ELIMINATE THE DUTY OF LOYALTY
California's limited partnership statute lists specific things a partnership agreement is not permitted to do, and one of them is eliminating the general partner's duty of loyalty defined in the duty-source statute discussed elsewhere in this document. The statute does, however, permit the partnership agreement to do two narrower things instead: identify specific categories of activity that do not violate the duty of loyalty, so long as doing so is not manifestly unreasonable, and specify what number or percentage of partners may authorize or ratify — after full disclosure of all material facts — a specific act or transaction that would otherwise violate the duty of loyalty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Eliminate the duty of loyalty under Section 15904.08, but the partnership agreement may do either or both of the following:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the partnership agreement may not eliminate the duty of loyalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15901.10.)
  "Identify specific types or categories of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, identifying non-violating categories of activity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15901.10.)
  "Specify the number or percentage of partners which may authorize or ratify, after full disclosure to all partners of all material facts, a specific act or transaction that otherwise would violate the duty of loyalty."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, authorization or ratification after full disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15901.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(5), including its two lettered sub-provisions. It does not define "manifestly unreasonable," a standard the statute leaves undefined, and it does not address the other thirteen restrictions the same subdivision (b) places on what a partnership agreement may vary, several of which are unrelated to fiduciary duty (for example, the power to sue and be sued, or the requirements for a certificate of limited partnership); this document addresses only the fiduciary-duty-related restrictions in paragraphs (5) through (7). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

WHAT THE PARTNERSHIP AGREEMENT MAY NOT DO: UNREASONABLY REDUCE CARE, OR ELIMINATE GOOD FAITH
The same statutory list of restrictions on a partnership agreement also addresses the duty of care and the good-faith-and-fair-dealing obligation. A partnership agreement may not unreasonably reduce the duty of care described elsewhere in this document. It also may not eliminate the good-faith-and-fair-dealing obligation, though the statute permits the partnership agreement to prescribe the standards by which performance of that obligation is measured, so long as the standards are not manifestly unreasonable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Unreasonably reduce the duty of care under subdivision (c) of Section 15904.08."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, no unreasonable reduction of the duty of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15901.10.)
  "Eliminate the obligation of good faith and fair dealing under subdivision (b) of Section 15903.05 and subdivision (d) of Section 15904.08, but the partnership agreement may prescribe the standards by which the performance of the obligation is to be measured, if the standards are not manifestly unreasonable."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text), California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, no elimination of the good faith and fair dealing obligation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=15901.10.)
  Known gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(6) and (b)(7). Unlike the loyalty restriction in paragraph (5), paragraph (6) permits some reduction of the duty of care — only an "unreasonable" reduction is barred — and the statute does not itself define the line between a reasonable and an unreasonable reduction. It does not address the other paragraphs of subdivision (b) beyond (5), (6), and (7). No case law was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search located no California opinion applying paragraph (6) or (7) to a specific partnership agreement provision.

PREPARATION AND SIGNATURE BLOCK
This information sheet regarding the fiduciary duties of Jordan Lee as general partner of Acme Ventures, LP was prepared by Jordan Lee.

Executed on September 8, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________
